arXiv:2602.13942v1 [stat.ML] 15 Feb 2026

A Theoretical Framework for LLM Fine-tuning Using Early Stopping for Non-random Initialization

Zexuan Sun Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: University of Wisconsin, Madison Affiliation: Madison, WI 53706 Email: zexuan.sun@wisc.edu    Garvesh Raskutti Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: University of Wisconsin, Madison Affiliation: Madison, WI 53706 Email: raskutti@stat.wisc.edu
Abstract

In the era of large language models (LLMs), fine-tuning pretrained models has become ubiquitous. Yet the theoretical underpinning remains an open question. A central question is why only a few epochs of fine-tuning are typically sufficient to achieve strong performance on many different tasks. In this work, we approach this question by developing a statistical framework, combining rigorous early stopping theory with the attention-based Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) for LLMs, offering new theoretical insights on fine-tuning practices. Specifically, we formally extend classical NTK theory (Jacot et al., 2018) to non-random (i.e., pretrained) initializations and provide a convergence guarantee for attention-based fine-tuning. One key insight provided by the theory is that the convergence rate with respect to sample size is closely linked to the eigenvalue decay rate of the empirical kernel matrix induced by the NTK. We also demonstrate how the framework can be used to explain task vectors for multiple tasks in LLMs. Finally, experiments with modern language models on real-world datasets provide empirical evidence supporting our theoretical insights.

   

A Preprint

Keywords: Early stopping, large language models, Neural Tangent Kernel, task vectors

1 Introduction

With the success of modern large language models (LLMs) (e.g. GPT models (Radford et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2020)), it has become standard practice to address supervised natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as topic classification, textual entailment and others by fine-tuning a pretrained model on a task-specific dataset (Joshi et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2020). Despite the strong empirical performance of this approach, our theoretical understanding of fine-tuning remains limited. A widely adopted convention in practice is to initialize with parameters from a pre-trained model and then do gradient updates for only a small number of epochs, typically between two and five, since empirical evidence suggests that longer training yields diminishing returns and may even increase the risk of overfitting (Stollenwerk, 2022). This naturally raises the question: why is a few epochs of fine-tuning sufficient? Intuitively, one might argue that pretrained models, having been exposed to vast text corpora, already provide strong representations. Yet a more formal and rigorous interpretation of this phenomenon is still lacking.

The vast number of parameters in modern models motivates the application of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory (Jacot et al., 2018) to the study of fine-tuning (Malladi et al., 2023). However, NTK theory alone is insufficient to capture the “early-stopping” phenomenon that is central to modern practice because it does not explain how changes in the data are captured by the NTK. To address this limitation, we build on theoretical advances in early stopping (Raskutti et al., 2014; Sun and Raskutti, 2025a) and apply to the LLM setting. In particular, Sun and Raskutti (2025a) combine early stopping with NTK theory to characterize the performance of wide fully connected neural networks and gradient boosting decision trees in estimating variable importance. This line of work suggests promising extensions to more complex network architectures in the context of modern fine-tuning.

In this paper, we consider a transformer-based network for regression learning problems to give a unique perspective of understanding modern fine-tuning for large models. Our major contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formally extend conventional infinite-width analysis to a multi-head attention-based network and our theory accounts for a pretrained initialization, which includes the stability of NTK during training and the linearization of the multi-head attention network (Lemma 1) in our setup.

  2. 2.

    We extend the theoretical framework in Sun and Raskutti (2025a) to transformer based network fine-tuning, which includes the setting where additional structure can be appended to certain hidden layers of the pretrained model (Theorem 1 and 2).

  3. 3.

    Based on the proven theoretical results, we give formal explanation of task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023), including negation and addition. And we recover the same weight disentanglement condition in Ortiz-Jimenez et al. (2023), which is claimed to be the only necessary condition for task vector to work (Section 5.2.2) .

  4. 4.

    We discuss the valuable insights offered by our proposed theoretical framework and connect them to real-world LLM fine-tuning practices (Section 6). We also conduct experiments with modern LLMs, specifically, the GPT-Neo model, to provide empirical evidence supporting our theoretical insights (Section 7).

2 RELATED WORK

Early stopping theory.

Early stopping has a long history (Anderssen and Prenter, 1981; Strand, 1974), with significant theoretical developments in classification boosting (Jiang, 2004; Zhang and Yu, 2005; Yao et al., 2007), L2-boosting (Bühlmann and Yu, 2003; Bühlmann and Hothorn, 2007), and gradient-based algorithms in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) (Vito et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2007; Raskutti et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2017; Sun and Raskutti, 2025a). Building on this line of work, the present paper extends the theoretical framework of early stopping in Sun and Raskutti (2025a), which focused on large fully connected networks, to more complex neural architectures. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first theoretical analysis that leverages early stopping theory in the context of fine-tuning.

Kernel view of neural networks.

Overparameterized models, including deep neural networks, are often analyzed through the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) framework (Jacot et al., 2018), which provides guarantees of global convergence (Arora et al., 2019; Allen-Zhu et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019a; Du et al., 2019b) and justifies linear approximations of network behavior (Lee et al., 2019), with extensions to convolutional architectures (Yang, 2020a). Subsequent work based on the Tensor Program framework generalized these results to a wide range of neural architectures (Yang, 2019; Yang and Littwin, 2021; Yang, 2020b). However, these analyses all rely on random Gaussian initialization of the weights. Malladi et al. (2023) extend the theory to non-random (i.e., pretrained) initialization under the assumption that the pretraining task is sufficiently related to the downstream task. Specifically, they assume that the gradient of the pretrained network with respect to the downstream task tends to zero as the width approaches infinity. In contrast, our work do not have this assumption and establishes similar theoretical guarantees under sufficiently large width and embedding dimension, relying on different proof techniques.

Task vector theory.

Proposed by Ilharco et al. (2023), task arithmetic has recently emerged as a cost-effective and scalable method for editing pretrained models directly in weight space. Subsequent work has sought to develop a theoretical understanding of this approach, for example by analyzing it through the lens of NTK theory (Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023) or by considering a conceptual learning setting in which each task corresponds to a binary classification problem defined by a discriminative pattern (Li et al., 2025). Notably, the explanation derived from our theoretical results aligns with the weight disentanglement condition introduced in (Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023).

3 BASIC SETUP AND PRELIMS

3.1 Statistical framework

In order to adapt to multiple scenarios, we consider a general learning setup. Assume that initially, we have source data (𝐗isrc,Yisrc),i=1,…,N1\left(\mathbf{X}^{\text{src}}_{i},Y^{\text{src}}_{i}\right),i=1,\ldots,N_{1} from (Xsrc,Ysrc)∼Psrc(X^{\text{src}},Y^{\text{src}})\sim P_{\text{src}} to train a pretrained model fPTf_{\text{PT}}. Next, we have data from our target (𝐗itgt,Yitgt),i=1,…,N1\left(\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{i},Y^{\text{tgt}}_{i}\right),i=1,\ldots,N_{1} from (Xtgt,Ytgt)∼Ptgt(X^{\text{tgt}},Y^{\text{tgt}})\sim P_{\text{tgt}}. The basic idea is using the pretrained model fPTf_{\text{PT}} as a starting point to model our target function ftgtf_{\text{tgt}} without the need to train a new model from scratch. More precisely, we plan to use fPTf_{\text{PT}} as initialization and train with (𝐗itgt,Yitgt)\left(\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{i},Y^{\text{tgt}}_{i}\right) to get the so-called fine-tuned model fFTf_{\text{FT}}. We use 𝑿src\bm{X}^{\text{src}}, 𝑿tgt\bm{X}^{\text{tgt}}, 𝒀src\bm{Y}^{\text{src}} and 𝒀tgt\bm{Y}^{\text{tgt}} to denote (𝐗1srcT,…,𝐗N1srcT)({\mathbf{X}^{\text{src}}_{1}}^{T},\dots,{\mathbf{X}^{\text{src}}_{N_{1}}}^{T}), (𝐗1tgtT,…,𝐗N2tgtT)({\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{1}}^{T},\dots,{\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{N_{2}}}^{T}), (Y1src,…,YN1src)T(Y^{\text{src}}_{1},\dots,Y^{\text{src}}_{N_{1}})^{T} and (Y1tgt,…,YN2tgt)T(Y^{\text{tgt}}_{1},\dots,Y^{\text{tgt}}_{N_{2}})^{T}, respectively.

We assume that the samples take the following form with respect to data XsrcX^{\text{src}} and XtgtX^{\text{tgt}} :

Yisrc=𝔼⁡[Yisrc∣Xisrc]+wisrc\displaystyle Y^{\text{src}}_{i}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}^{\text{src}}\mid X_{i}^{\text{src}}]+w^{\text{src}}_{i} (1)
Yitgt=𝔼⁡[Yitgt∣Xitgt]+witgt\displaystyle Y^{\text{tgt}}_{i}=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i}^{\text{tgt}}\mid X_{i}^{\text{tgt}}\right]+w_{i}^{\text{tgt}}

To assess how well the approximation ftgt^\widehat{f_{\text{tgt}}} matches the target function ftgtf_{\text{tgt}}, we mainly consider L2​(P)L^{2}(P)-norm:

‖ftgt^−ftgt‖22=𝔼⁡[(ftgt^​(𝐗tgt)−ftgt​(𝐗tgt))2]\left\|\widehat{f_{\text{tgt}}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\widehat{f_{\text{tgt}}}(\mathbf{X^{\text{tgt}}})-f_{\text{tgt}}(\mathbf{X^{\text{tgt}}})\right)^{2}\right] (2)

3.3 Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

To analyze early stopping in kernel-based methods, we rely on the framework of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (Aronszajn, 1950). Specifically, consider a Hilbert space ℋ⊂L2​(P)\mathcal{H}\subset L^{2}(P) consisting of functions g:𝒳→ℝg:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} with ‖g‖L2​(P)<∞\|g\|_{L^{2}(P)}<\infty, equipped with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℋ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} under which ℋ\mathcal{H} is complete. The space ℋ\mathcal{H} is an RKHS if there exists a symmetric kernel function 𝕂:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}{+} such that (a) for each x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the function 𝕂⁡(⋅,x)\mathbb{K}(\cdot,x) belongs to ℋ\mathcal{H}, and (b) the reproducing property holds: f⁡(x)=⟨f,𝕂⁡(⋅,x)⟩​ℋf(x)=\langle f,\mathbb{K}(\cdot,x)\rangle{\mathcal{H}} for all f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H}. Such a kernel function is required to be positive semidefinite.

For a specific kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} on data XX, we define the entries of the associated empirical kernel matrix KK as follows:

K⁡(i,j)=1N​𝕂​(𝐗i,𝐗j).K(i,j)=\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{K}(\mathbf{X}_{i},\mathbf{X}_{j}). (5)

As stated in Sun and Raskutti (2025a), The empirical kernel matrix is fundamental to our theoretical analysis, providing the basis for reparameterizing the gradient update equation and deriving the optimal early stopping rule.

3.4 Neural Tangent Kernel

The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), first introduced by Jacot et al. (2018), serves as a theoretical framework for analyzing neural networks within the RKHS setting. Denote the neural network by f⁡(θ,x)f(\theta,x), its Neural Tangent Kernel is defined as

⟨∇θf​(θ,x),∇θf​(θ,x′)⟩.\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta,x\right),\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta,x^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle. (6)

A large body of theoretical results has been established for neural networks under random normal initialization and in the infinite-width regime. In this setting, it is well known that the NTK remains constant throughout training, and the initial kernel converges in probability to a deterministic limiting kernel (add reference later). (Sun and Raskutti, 2025a) extend these results to warm-start initialization for fully connected networks. For the network considered in this paper, we aim to get similar results, which enables us to build a theoretical framework to explain modern deep learning fine-tuning.

In particular, at each iteration, the network fτf_{\tau} induces a corresponding NTK, denoted by 𝕂τ\mathbb{K}_{\tau}. This kernel will converge to a stationary kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} as the width goes to infinity. In particular, the functional form is determined by the structure of the network, not by the input training data (Sun and Raskutti, 2025a).

In this paper, we formally show that for networks including transformer decoders with pre-trained initialization, the NTK remains stable during training when the width and hidden dimension are sufficiently large. The challenging part of extension to including transformer decoder is to deal with the multi-head attention.

Denote the Jacobian of the network evaluated on the data 𝑿tgt\bm{X}^{\text{tgt}} as J⁡(θ)∈ℝN2×|θ|J(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{2}\times|\theta|}. The empirical kernel matrix is can be expressed as

K=1N2​J​(θ)​J​(θ)⊤.K=\frac{1}{N_{2}}J(\theta)J(\theta)^{\top}. (7)

The calculation of gradient becomes more complicated after introducing attention. Consider layer ll to be the an multi-head attention layer. We define the following intermediate quantities:

Qh=gl−1Wl​h,Q,Kh=gl−1Wl​h,K,Vh=gl−1Wl​h,V,\displaystyle Q_{h}=g^{l-1}W^{lh,Q},\quad K_{h}=g^{l-1}W^{lh,K},\quad V_{h}=g^{l-1}W^{lh,V}, (8)
Sh=1dl,GQhKh⊤,Ph=softmaxrows(Sh),Ah=PhVh,\displaystyle S_{h}=\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}Q_{h}K_{h}^{\top},\quad P_{h}=\operatorname{softmax}_{\mathrm{rows}}(S_{h}),\quad A_{h}=P_{h}V_{h},
Λh=block​_​diag⁡(Λh,0,…,Λh,T−1)∈ℝT2×T2,\displaystyle\Lambda_{h}=\operatorname{block\_diag}\left(\Lambda_{h,0},\ldots,\Lambda_{h,T-1}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{2}\times T^{2}},
Λh,i=diag(Ph,i:)−Ph,i:Ph,i:⊤.\displaystyle\Lambda_{h,i}=\operatorname{diag}\left(P_{h,i:}\right)-P_{h,i:}P_{h,i:}^{\top}.

Then the Jacobian w.r.t. the attention weights is:

J⁡(Wl​h,V)=gl−1⊤​Ph⊤​∂fL+1∂fl​h​Wl​h,O⊤\displaystyle J(W^{lh,V})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}P_{h}^{\top}\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial f^{lh}}{W^{lh,O}}^{\top} (9)
J⁡(Wl,O)=[fl​1​(x),…,fl​dl,H​(x)]T​∂fL+1∂fl\displaystyle J(W^{l,O})=\left[f^{l1}(x),\ldots,f^{ld^{l,H}}(x)\right]^{T}\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial f^{l}}
J⁡(Wl​h,Q)=gl−1⊤⋅(1dl,G⋅∂Ph∂Sh⊤⋅∂fL+1∂Ph⋅Kh)\displaystyle J(W^{lh,Q})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\cdot{\frac{\partial P_{h}}{\partial S_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial P_{h}}\cdot K^{h}\right)
J⁡(Wl​h,K)=gl−1⊤⋅(1dl,G⋅∂fL+1∂Ph⊤⋅∂Ph∂Sh⊤⋅Qh)\displaystyle J(W^{lh,K})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\cdot{\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial P_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot{\frac{\partial P_{h}}{\partial S_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot Q^{h}\right)

As the expression shows, the special added structure adds up the mathematical expressions and we need to take care of them during the following theoretical analysis.

3.5 Early stopping with data-dependent stopping rule

Early stopping is a key regularization technique in deep learning, typically determined via a hold-out set in practice. Although the exact optimal time is intractable, data-dependent rules provide theoretical insight (Raskutti et al., 2014; Sun and Raskutti, 2025a).

The rule depends on the empirical kernel matrix K∈ℝN2×N2K\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{2}\times N_{2}} from kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} on XtgtX^{\text{tgt}}, with eigenvalues {λ^i}i=1N2\{\widehat{\lambda}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{2}}. Define the local empirical Rademacher complexity (Raskutti et al., 2014):

ℛ^K​(ϱ):=[1N​∑i=1Nmin⁡{λ^i,ϱ2}]1/2\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{K}(\varrho):=\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\min\left\{\widehat{\lambda}_{i},\varrho^{2}\right\}\right]^{1/2} (10)

For noise variance σ>0\sigma>0, the critical empirical radius ϱ^N\widehat{\varrho}_{N} is the smallest positive solution solving

ℛ^K​(ϱ)≤ϱ2​Cℋ22​e​σ\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{K}(\varrho)\leq\frac{\varrho^{2}C_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{2e\sigma} (11)

with Cℋ=‖fPT−ftgt‖ℋC_{\mathcal{H}}=\|f_{\text{PT}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}. The stopping threshold T^max\widehat{T}_{\max} is well-defined, and the optimal time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} minimizes a bound on the empirical L2​(P)L^{2}(P) norm for τ≤T^max\tau\leq\widehat{T}_{\max} (Sun and Raskutti, 2025b).

4 THEORETICAL GUARANTEES

We fist consider an easier case where the pre-trained model fPTf_{\text{PT}} has the same architecture as the fine-tuned model fFTf_{\text{FT}} , including width, number of layers, and hidden dimension and establish a convergence result for it (Section 4.2). This theoretical result is then used to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the empirical success of modern fine-tuning methods. Subsequently, we extend the analysis to encompass more general fine-tuning regimes that permit the incorporation of additional structural components to better accommodate a range of downstream tasks (Section 5.1). Finally, under appropriate additional assumptions, we utilize the proposed framework to provide a theoretical explanation of task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023).

4.1 Assumptions

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote the RKHS induced by the stationary kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} on XtgtX^{\text{tgt}}, and denote the Hilbert norm in ℋ\mathcal{H} by ∥⋅∥ℋ\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}}. We require the following basic assumptions for our theory.

Assumption 4.1.

fPT−ftgtf_{\text{PT}}-f_{\text{tgt}} belongs to ℋ\mathcal{H}, i.e., fPT−ftgt∈span​{𝕂⁡(⋅,Xtgt)}f_{\text{PT}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\in\text{span}\{\mathbb{K}(\cdot,X^{\text{tgt}})\}.

This assumption is made for purely theoretical convenience avoiding the need to add additional mis-specification error terms or do projections.

Assumption 4.2.

The data {(𝐗isrc,Yisrc)}i=1N1\left\{(\mathbf{X}^{\text{src}}_{i},Y^{\text{src}}_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{1}}, and {(𝐗itgt,Yitgt)}i=1N2\left\{(\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{i},Y^{\text{tgt}}_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{2}} are contained in closed and bounded set in ℝp+1\mathbb{R}^{p+1}.

Assumption 4.3.

witgtw_{i}^{\text{tgt}} are independent zero-mean random variables satisfying the following sub-Gaussianity condition:

𝔼⁡[et​witgt]≤et2​σ2/2, for all ​t∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}\left[e^{tw_{i}^{\text{tgt}}}\right]\leq e^{t^{2}\sigma^{2}/2},\text{ for all }t\in\mathbb{R}. (12)

It is well known that boundedness is a sufficient condition for sub-Gaussianity.

Assumption 4.4.

The dropout error does satisfies ‖𝐘tgt−fPT​(𝐗tgt)‖2=O⁡(N)\|\bm{Y^{\text{tgt}}}-f_{\text{PT}}(\bm{X}^{\text{tgt}})\|_{2}=O(\sqrt{N}).

This condition effectively ensures that the initialization using the pre-trained model is reasonable

Assumption 4.5.

The empirical kernel matrix induced by the stationary NTK, as width and hidden dimension dl→∞d^{l}\rightarrow\infty, KK is full rank.

Assumption 4.6.

The activation function ϕ\phi satisfies

|ϕ⁡(0)|,‖ϕ′‖∞,supx≠x~|ϕ′​(x)−ϕ′​(x~)|/|x−x~|<∞.|\phi(0)|,\quad\left\|\phi^{\prime}\right\|_{\infty},\quad\sup_{x\neq\tilde{x}}\left|\phi^{\prime}(x)-\phi^{\prime}(\tilde{x})\right|/|x-\tilde{x}|<\infty. (13)
Assumption 4.7.

The pretrained model fPTf_{\text{PT}} is trained starting from weights drawn from a normal random initialization.

4.2 Fine-tuning

Our analysis relies critically on the linearization of the network under consideration. While such linearization results are well established in the context of over-parameterized networks (Lee et al., 2019), our setting differs in that we allow non-random initialization and focus on architectures with transformer blocks.

As a useful intermediate results, we prove the network linearization rigorously in the pretrained initialization, which is crucial for helping derive the final theoretical bounds. This result can also be applied to interpret the success of task arithmetic (Section 5.2).

Lemma 1 (Network linearization).

Under the setup in this paper, we are able to linearize the fine-tuned network around the pretrained model fPTf_{\text{PT}}, i.e., we have

fFT\displaystyle f_{\text{FT}} =fPT+Δθ∇fPT(θ)+e\displaystyle=f_{\text{PT}}+\Delta\theta\nabla f_{\text{PT}}(\theta)+e (14)
=fPT+∑iζi​𝕂​(⋅,𝐗i)+e\displaystyle=f_{\text{PT}}+\sum_{i}\zeta_{i}\mathbb{K}(\cdot,\mathbf{X}_{i})+e

where the L2L_{2}-norm of the error term ee is bounded by 𝒪~​(1dl1/2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{1}{{d^{l}}^{1/2}}\right).

Theorem 1.

Consider a network described in Section 3.2 and has identical architecture as fPTf_{\text{PT}} , under assumptions in Section 4.1, for any γ>0\gamma>0, there exists sufficient large width and embedding dimension MM, such that the following bounds hold with probability at least 1−γ−c1​exp⁡(−c2​N2​ϱ^N2)1-\gamma-c_{1}\exp(-c_{2}N_{2}\widehat{\varrho}_{N_{2}}) when fine-tuning the pretrained model fPTf_{\text{PT}} on the target dataset XtgtX^{\text{tgt}} using gradient descent with learning rate ϵ=O⁡(1dl)\epsilon=O(\frac{1}{d^{l}}):

‖fT^o​p−ftgt‖22\displaystyle\|f_{\widehat{T}_{op}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\|_{2}^{2} ≤𝒪⁡(N2−12).\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\left(N_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right). (15)

where c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are some universal positive constants.

Proof sketch.

The proof of this result relies heavily on the proof strategy in Sun and Raskutti (2025b) for fully connected networks adapted to the attention-based network. Compared with Sun and Raskutti (2025b), the major difference of our paper is that we consider transformer decoder, which presents significantly more theoretical challenges due to the complexity of the Jacobian matrix discussed earlier.

One of the key intermediate results we need to prove is the local Lipschitzness of the Jacobian for the network under random normal initialization, which will later be extended to pre-trained initialization. The challenges come mainly from dealing with attention weights. After adding this complicated module, when considering the Jacobian of other fully connected weights, we need to be careful about the effects brought about by attention weights. In particular for attention weights, we need to show that

‖J⁡(Wl​h,∙)‖F≤O⁡(dl1/2)\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,\bullet})\right\|_{F}\leq O({d^{l}}^{1/2}) (16)
‖J⁡(Wl​h,∙)​(θ,x)−J⁡(Wl​h,∙)​(θ~,x)‖F≤𝒪~​(dl1/2)​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,\bullet})(\theta,x)-J(W^{lh,\bullet})(\tilde{\theta},x)\right\|_{F}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({d^{l}}^{1/2})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}

where ∙∈{Q,K,V,O}\bullet\in\{Q,K,V,O\}.

Recall the expression for the Jacobian of attention weights in 9, to get the final bounds, we need to prove the boundness and local lipschitzness of all the elements inside those expressions. And this replies on the induction results from previous and later layers. After this major step, we need the following steps to derive the final bound:

  1. 1.

    Based on the local Lipschitzness of the Jacobian, we prove the NTK stability, network linearlization for pre-trained network fPTf_{\text{PT}} under random random initialization and show that the parameter of fPTf_{\text{PT}} is not far away from the random initialized network frandom_initf_{\text{random\_init}}. Specifically, let θ0\theta_{0} denote the parameter of frandom_initf_{\text{random\_init}} and θPT\theta_{\text{PT}} denote that of fPTf_{\text{PT}}. We formally show that θPT\theta_{\text{PT}} lies in the neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0} with controlled radius, which is B(θ0,C1n−1/2)B(\theta_{0},C_{1}n^{-1/2}), where nn is the width or hidden dimension of the network. .

  2. 2.

    Based on previous step 1, we prove the local Lipschitzness of the Jacobian under the pre-trained initialization. The core idea of to prove this is to use the proved result is step 1, i.e.m the parameter of pre-trained network θP​T\theta_{PT} is within the B⁡(θ0,C1​dl−12)B(\theta_{0},C_{1}{d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}) neighbor of some random weights θ0\theta_{0}, then for any θ,θ~∈B⁡(θPT,C2​dl−12)\theta,\tilde{\theta}\in B(\theta_{\text{PT}},C_{2}{d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}), they also belong to a neighbor of θ0\theta_{0}, i.e. , B⁡(θ0,C3​dl−12)B(\theta_{0},C_{3}{d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}) with a larger constant C3C_{3}. then by the local Lipschitzness of the random weights, we can get the local Lipschitzness under pre-trained initialization. This process is visualized Figure 1.

  3. 3.

    Based on Step 2, we establish NTK stability and network linearization for the pre-trained initialization using a proof strategy similar to that in Sun and Raskutti (2025a); Sun and Raskutti (2025b). More formally, we show that the empirical kernel remains nearly constant throughout training; that is,

    supτ‖KPT−Kτ‖F≤𝒪⁡(dl−12)\sup_{\tau}\left\|K_{\text{PT}}-K_{\tau}\right\|_{F}\leq\mathcal{O}({d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}) (17)

    Moreover, the fine-tuned network fFTf_{\text{FT}} can be linearized around the pre-trained network fPTf_{\text{PT}} as

    fFT≈fPT+Δθ∇fPT(θ).f_{\text{FT}}\approx f_{\text{PT}}+\Delta\theta\nabla f_{\text{PT}}(\theta). (18)
  4. 4.

    Based on Step 3, we establish a convergence bound for the optimal stopping rule T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} under gradient descent by leveraging proof techniques from Raskutti et al. (2014); Sun and Raskutti (2025a); Sun and Raskutti (2025b), which are specifically developed for the rigorous theoretical analysis of early stopping. Roughly speaking, the proof begins by decomposing the empirical normal of the mean prediction error as

    ‖fτ−ftgt‖N22≤Bτ2+Vτ+Dτ2\left\|f_{\tau}-f_{\text{tgt}}\right\|_{N_{2}}^{2}\leq B_{\tau}^{2}+V_{\tau}+D_{\tau}^{2} (19)

    where Bτ2B_{\tau}^{2} is the bias term, VτV_{\tau} is the variance term and Dτ2D_{\tau}^{2} is the additional discrepancy term induced by the kernel variation during network training. We then bound each of these three terms at the desired rate, namely 𝒪⁡(dl−12)\mathcal{O}({d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}). Finally, we control the difference between the population 22-norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} and the empirical norm ∥⋅∥N\|\cdot\|_{N} to obtain the final convergence bound stated in Theorem 1.

The technical details of each step are deferred to the supplementary materials.

∎

Remark 4.1.

In the original NTK paper (Jacot et al., 2018), the NTK is analyzed under the assumption of infinite width. In the infinite-width (or infinite hidden-dimension) regime, the change of the NTK during training converges to 00, and consequently the difference term Dτ2D_{\tau}^{2} in the error bound vanishes. In contrast, our setup does not require such a strong assumption. Instead, we bound the NTK variation during training using concentration inequalities with respect to dld^{l}. And we only require dld^{l} to be sufficiently large to ensure that Dτ2D_{\tau}^{2} is bounded by 𝒪⁡(dl−12)\mathcal{O}({d^{l}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}).

5 Specific fine-tuning settings

In this section, we focus on two particular settings where fine-tuning is used in LLMs: linear probing and multitask learning with task arithmetic.

5.1 General Fine-tuning and Linear Probing

We now turn to a more general fine-tuning setup. Specifically, suppose we retain only the last kk layers of the pretrained model as a backbone, denoted with fPTkf_{\text{PT}}^{k} and append a linear head tailored to a new downstream task. The linear head is initialized with random Gaussian weights. During fine-tuning, we update the parameters of both the backbone and the newly added linear head (Kumar et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).

This setting is closer to standard practice, since in most cases the output layer of the pretrained model does not align with that of the target task. The main theoretical challenge, however, lies in the fact that the initialization now combines non-random initialization (from the pre-trained backbone) with random initialization (from the newly added head), a regime for which existing results are not directly applicable. Since we only use the first kk layer of fPTf_{\text{PT}}, the quantity CℋC_{\mathcal{H}} becomes

‖LinearHead​(fPTk)−ftgt‖ℋ\left\|\text{LinearHead}(f^{k}_{\text{PT}})-f_{\text{tgt}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}} (20)

Then we can achieve similar theoretical result as follows:

Theorem 2.

Consider a fine-tuning setting described above, under assumptions in Section 4.1, for any γ>0\gamma>0, there exists sufficient large width and embedding dimension dld^{l}, such that the following bounds hold with probability at least 1−γ−c1​exp⁡(−c2​N2​ϱ^N2)1-\gamma-c_{1}\exp(-c_{2}N_{2}\widehat{\varrho}_{N_{2}}), when fine-tuning starting from fPTkf_{\text{PT}}^{k} and add an additional linear head using gradient descent with learning rate ϵ=O⁡(1dl)\epsilon=O(\frac{1}{d^{l}}):

‖fT^o​p−ftgt‖22\displaystyle\|f_{\widehat{T}_{op}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\|_{2}^{2} ≤𝒪⁡(N2−12).\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\left(N_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right). (21)

The overall proof framework is the same as Theorem 1, but we need to adapt to the mixed initialization.

Remark 5.1.

Linear probing freezes the backbone and trains only the head, reducing the problem to passing inputs through the backbone and solving a standard linear regression. In this case, the classical framework of Raskutti et al. (2014) applies directly, yielding analogous convergence results.

5.2 Task Arithmetic

For a particular task, the task vector τ\tau is defined as the difference between fPTf_{\text{PT}} and fFTf_{\text{FT}} (Ilharco et al., 2023). Specifically,

τ=θFT−θPT.\tau=\theta_{\text{FT}}-\theta_{\text{PT}}. (22)

In this section, we demonstrate how are fine-tuning approach yields similar results to prior work done on task arithmetic. We consider two types of task arithmetic: i) negation: users can negate a task vector to degrade performance on certain task, ii) addition: adding task vectors can help build better multi-task models.

5.2.1 Negation

To negate a task vector, we simply set the parameter of the negating network fnegf_{\text{neg}} as

θneg=θFT−τ.\theta_{\text{neg}}=\theta_{\text{FT}}-\tau. (23)

Applying Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, it is straightforward to obtain the following result.

Corollary 1.

For the network considered in this paper, under assumptions in Section 4.1 , for any γ>0\gamma>0, there exist sufficiently large width and embedding dimension, when starting from fPTf_{\text{PT}} and using gradient descent with ϵ=O⁡(1dl)\epsilon=O(\frac{1}{d^{l}}), the expected MSE of fnegf_{\text{neg}} is larger than that of fFTf_{\text{FT}} with probability at least 1−γ−c5​exp⁡(−c6​N2​ϱ^N2)1-\gamma-c_{5}\exp(-c_{6}N_{2}\widehat{\varrho}_{N_{2}}) , i.e.

𝔼⁡[M​S​E​(fneg)]−𝔼⁡[M​S​E​(fFT)]>0.\mathbb{E}[MSE(f_{\text{neg}})]-\mathbb{E}[MSE(f_{\text{FT}})]>0. (24)

5.2.2 Addition

Suppose we want to use the task vector to build a multi-task model fMultiTaskf_{\text{MultiTask}}. For simplicity we consider two different tasks. Let the data for these two tasks as Xtask1X^{\text{task}_{1}} and Xtask2X^{\text{task}_{2}}. We add the below assumption:

Assumption 5.1.

the Hilbert space of span​{𝕂⁡(⋅,Xtask1)}\text{span}\{\mathbb{K}(\cdot,X^{\text{task}_{1}})\} and span​{𝕂⁡(⋅,Xtask2)}\text{span}\{\mathbb{K}(\cdot,X^{\text{task}_{2}})\} are orthogonal.

This assumption seems quite strong, but task vectors are almost orthogonal according to the experiments in Ilharco et al. (2023). Note that this is a sufficient condition for task addition to work, if this do not hold, we cannot argue that task addition will lead to poor performance.

Denote the task vector for task 1 and 2 as τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2}, respectively. We have the following result.

Corollary 2.

For the network considered in this paper, under assumption 5.1, and assumptions in Section 4.1, we are able to recover the disentanglement condition in Ortiz-Jimenez et al. (2023). Specifically, for any γ>0\gamma>0, there exists sufficient large width and em- bedding dimension dld^{l}, such that the following holds with probability at least 1−r1-r staring from fPTf_{\text{PT}} with learning rate ϵ=O⁡(1dl)\epsilon=O(\frac{1}{d^{l}}):

fMultiTask\displaystyle f_{\text{MultiTask}} =f⁡(X,θPT+∑i=12τi)\displaystyle=f\left(X,\theta_{\text{PT}}+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\tau_{i}\right) (25)
=∑i=22gi​(X,τi)+fPT+e\displaystyle=\sum_{i=2}^{2}g_{i}(X,\tau_{i})+f_{\text{PT}}+e

where gi​(𝐗,τi)=0g_{i}(\mathbf{X},\tau_{i})=0 for 𝐗∉Xtaski\mathbf{X}\notin X^{\text{task}_{i}}. And the L2L_{2} norm of the error term ee is bounded by 𝒪~​(1dl1/2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{1}{{d^{l}}^{1/2}}\right).

6 Practical Insights

Although the optimal stopping time T^o​p\widehat{T}_{op} is not directly computable in practice, the theoretical results provide a principled abstraction that yields concrete and actionable insights for real-world LLM fine-tuning after a closer examination.

6.1 The theoretical framework encourages stopping early

As for the question “why we only need a few epochs to get a good performance model?". We are able to answer it after reviewing more details of the theoretical optimal stopping time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}}. As mentioned in Section 3.5, we first define a threshold T^max\widehat{T}_{\max}. Then T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} is obtained by maximizing

Cϵ​τ+g⁡(τ)\frac{C}{\epsilon\tau}+g(\tau) (26)

where g⁡(τ)g(\tau) is an error term introduced by the accumulated kernel change during training and is non-decreasing with training epoch τ\tau. The rationale for limiting training to only a few epochs emerges from two aspects of the theory. First, recall that the constant CℋC_{\mathcal{H}} constrains T^max\widehat{T}_{\max} from being a large number, reflecting the expectation that fPTf_{\text{PT}} is already reasonably close to ftgtf_{\text{tgt}}. Second, the error term g⁡(τ)g(\tau) favors fewer iterations, since running too long leads to greater accumulation of errors.

6.2 Connection to kernel ridge regression

Early stopping is a classical method to prevent overfitting. And it has been shown that it is theoretically equivalent to kernel ridge regression in non-parametric regression settings (Raskutti et al., 2014). More specifically, the running sum of early stopping steps ϵ​T^\epsilon\widehat{T} acts the same as the ridge parameter λ\lambda in the kernel ridge regression theoretically. Later works (Gao et al., 2022; Sun and Raskutti, 2025a; Sun and Raskutti, 2025b) extend this result to fully connected neural networks. We can apply similar reasoning in our case to derive the theoretical equivalence between the early stopping and kernel ridge regression even though we consider way more complicated network structure.

Formally, the early stopping can be roughly viewed as solving the below ridge regression problem:

Δ​θ=arg⁡minω​1N2​∑i=1N2[Yitgt−fPT​(𝐗itgt)−wT​∇θfPT​(𝐗itgt)]2+λ​‖w‖22\Delta\theta=\arg\min_{\omega}\frac{1}{N_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{2}}\left[Y^{\text{tgt}}_{i}-f_{\text{PT}}(\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{i})-w^{T}\nabla_{\theta}f_{\text{PT}}(\mathbf{X}^{\text{tgt}}_{i})\right]^{2}+\lambda\|w\|^{2}_{2} (27)

where λ=ϵ​T^op\lambda=\epsilon\widehat{T}_{\text{op}}. Then the fine-tuned model can viewed roughly as

fFT≈fPT+Δθ∇fPT(θ).f_{\text{FT}}\approx f_{\text{PT}}+\Delta\theta\nabla f_{\text{PT}}(\theta). (28)

In Gao et al. (2022), the regularization parameter λ\lambda is chosen via k-fold cross validation. The optimal stopping time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} can only be computed under ideal theoretical settings. So in practice, we recommend using the hold-out method, where the training data is split into a validation set, and updates are halted when the validation loss shows no improvement over several iterations. Holdout early stopping can be loosely viewed as a degenerate case of cross-validation with a single validation split, but unlike k-fold cross validation, the validation data directly affects the training trajectory by determining the stopping time. Even though we adopt the hold-out method in our experiments, the optimal stopping rule proposed in the theoretical framework is expected to outperform the hold-out method, which is supported by simulations (Figure 3) in Raskutti et al. (2014).

6.3 Task specific convergence rate

The convergence rate established in Theorem 1 should be interpreted as an upper bound. In practice, the actual convergence behavior depends on the specific downstream task and the underlying network architecture (Sun and Raskutti, 2025b; Raskutti et al., 2014). In particular, it is closely tied to the eigenvalue decay rate of the population kernel matrix.

According to Sun and Raskutti (2025b), for neural networks one typically expects a polynomial eigenvalue decay, that is,

λk≤C​(1k)2​βfor some ​β>12​ constant ​C.\lambda_{k}\leq C(\frac{1}{k})^{2\beta}\ \ \quad\text{for some }\beta>\frac{1}{2}\text{ constant }C. (29)

Under this condition, the resulting convergence rate of the mean prediction error is expected to satisfy

‖fT^o​p−ftgt‖22\displaystyle\|f_{\widehat{T}_{op}}-f_{\text{tgt}}\|_{2}^{2} ≤𝒪⁡(N2−2​β2​β+1)\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\left(N_{2}^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}\right) (30)

This implies that for sufficiently large β\beta, the convergence rate approaches the parametric rate of 1/N21/N_{2}.

From a practical perspective, this result indicates that when comparing two downstream tasks with different eigenvalue decay rates, the task with faster decay can achieve comparable predictive performance using fewer training samples (up to constant factors). Consequently, the eigenvalue decay rate can serve as an informative measure of task–model compatibility in real-world fine-tuning scenarios. In particular, tasks exhibiting faster eigenvalue decay may require fewer labeled samples to reach a desired performance level for a given pre-trained model. We further illustrate these insights empirically in the experiment (Section 7.1 ).

7 EXPERIMENTS

To support our theoretical results, we conduct experiments using open-source GPT models whose architectures align with our setting. In particular, we use GPT-Neo-1.3B (16 heads, 128-dimensional embeddings), both pretrained on 825 GiB of text from 22 diverse sources (Black et al., 2021; Black et al., 2022).

We consider several NLP tasks, which cover: semantic textual similarity (STS-B (Cer et al., 2017), STS-2012(Agirre et al., 2012)), semantic textual relatedness (SemRel (Ousidhoum et al., 2024a; Ousidhoum et al., 2024b) ) natural language inference (RTE), sentiment analysis (CR, SentEval-CR (Ding et al., 2008), Amazon Polarity(McAuley and Leskovec, 2013)), paraphrase detection tasks (MRPC (Dolan and Brockett, 2005)). STS-B and STS-2012 are regression tasks and others are classification tasks. So we need to add an additional classification head to the GPTNeo models, so this falls into the specific fine-tuned setting discussed in Section 5.1.

As noted in Sun and Raskutti (2025a), the optimal stopping time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} is not computable in practice, so we adopt the same hold-out method to decide when to stop. In our experiments, we first investigate relationship between the eigenvalue decay and the fine-tuned model performance, and then show that when task vectors are nearly orthogonal across different tasks, task addition yields a multitask model fMultiTaskf_{\text{MultiTask}} with strong performance.

7.1 Eigenvalue decay rate investigation

We illustrate the connection between the eigenvalue decay rate and model performance using three regression tasks: SemRel, STS-B and STS 2012, and three classification tasks: RTE, MRPC, and Amazon Reviews. Specifically, we randomly select 100 samples from each fine-tuning dataset and compute the empirical kernel matrix induced by the NTK of fPTf_{\text{PT}}. We then fit a least-squares line to the log–log eigenvalue curve to estimate the polynomial decay coefficient β\beta in Equation (29).

For the regression tasks, the estimated mean decay rates are β=0.60±0.0366\beta=0.60\pm 0.0366 for SemRel , β=0.58±0.0126\beta=0.58\pm 0.0126 for STS-12 and 0.54±0.02290.54\pm 0.0229 for STS-B. For the classification tasks, the corresponding values are β=0.62±0.0076\beta=0.62\pm 0.0076, 0.55±0.00290.55\pm 0.0029, and 0.51±0.010.51\pm 0.01 for Amazon Reviews, MRPC, and RTE, respectively. The eigenvalue decay curves are reported in the Appendix. As discussed in Section 6.1, this predicts that fewer training samples are required for SemRel than for STS-12, and fewer for STS-12 than for STS-B, consistent with the fact that STS-12 is a cleaner subset of the data sources aggregated into STS-B. Similar conclusions are expected to hold for the three classification tasks.

We verify this prediction by evaluating fine-tuning performance under varying training sample sizes. For regression tasks, test performance is measured by MSE loss, while for classification tasks it is measured by test accuracy, as shown in Figure 2. The F1-score comparison for classification tasks is depicted in Figure 10 in the Appendix. For the regression tasks, we observe that SemRel performs best, followed by STS-2012, with STS-B performing the worst. Across all tasks, Amazon Reviews converges the fastest, reaching near-optimal performance with fewer than 500 training samples, followed by MRPC, while RTE exhibits the slowest convergence and the lowest overall performance. These results provide empirical support for the claims made in Section 6.1.

7.2 Task Vector

We primarily use GPT-Neo 1.3B in this experiment, as its setup aligns more closely with our theoretical assumptions. For a task pair (task1,task2)(\text{task}_{1},\text{task}_{2}), we first fine-tune the model separately on each task to obtain fFT1f_{\text{FT}_{1}} and fFT2f_{\text{FT}_{2}}. From these, we derive the corresponding task vectors τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2}. The multi-task model is then constructed by adding τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} to the pre-trained parameters fPTf_{\text{PT}} via task vector addition. We compute the cosine similarity between τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} across four datasets and compare the performance of fMultiTaskf_{\text{MultiTask}} against the individually fine-tuned models (Figure 3).

We observe that the task vector of RTE is nearly orthogonal to the other task vectors, and fMultiTaskf_{\text{MultiTask}} achieves strong performance on individual tasks, which is consistent with Corollary 2. Another key finding is that even when task vectors are not orthogonal, task addition can still yield good performance for fMultiTaskf_{\text{MultiTask}}. Importantly, we do not claim that correlation between task vectors or tasks necessarily leads to failure of task addition, so this observation does not contradict our theoretical results.

8 DISCUSSION

In this paper, we focus on transformer-based networks and establish a theoretical connection between modern fine-tuning practices and early stopping. Our analysis provides valuable practical insights about LLM finetuning from a rigorous perspective. The theoretical results also offer a more formal interpretation of the effectiveness of task arithmetic. While our work emphasizes a theoretical perspective, experiments with modern LLMs further support the analysis, highlighting the practical relevance of our framework.

The alignment between our theoretical predictions and the widespread success of pre-trained models in practice suggests that the proposed framework has the potential to extend to broader settings. In particular, it may accommodate alternative loss functions, additional components of modern deep learning architectures, and more advanced training techniques.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Datasets

The CR and SentEval-CR datasets are from Ding et al. [2008], MRPC is from [Dolan and Brockett, 2005], RTE is from Dagan et al. [2005] Amazon reviews dataset is from McAuley and Leskovec [2013], SST-12 is from Agirre et al. [2012] and STS-B is from Cer et al. [2017].

A.2 Computing the Kernel

We employ functorch [He and Zou, 2021] to compute the NTK for GPT-Neo 125M and GPT-Neo 1.3B, combining backward-mode automatic differentiation to obtain Jacobians with forward-mode differentiation to evaluate Jacobian–vector products [Novak et al., 2022].

A.3 Additional experiment results

The eigenvalue decay curves for different tasks are shown in Figure 4 – 9. The process to get the estimated β\beta is as follows. Suppose the eigenvalues follow a power law:

λk≈λ1​k−2​β\lambda_{k}\approx\lambda_{1}k^{-2\beta} (31)

taking logs:

log⁡(λk/λ1)≈−2​β​log⁡k\log(\lambda_{k}/\lambda_{1})\approx-2\beta\log k (32)

we then run a least square estimate on the log ration log⁡(λk/λ1)\log(\lambda_{k}/\lambda_{1}) and log⁡k\log k to estimate the slope −2​β-2\beta.

The f1 score comparison for the three classification tasks are shown in Figure 10. We can see that we observe similar pattern as the accuracy learning curve.

Appendix B Theoretical Results

B.1 Optimal Stopping Rule Details

The optimal stopping rule T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} mentioned in Section 3.5 of the main text is adopted directly from Sun and Raskutti [2025a]. Before discussing its details, we first define the L2​(PN)L^{2}\left(P_{N}\right)-norm as:

‖f^−f∗‖N2=1N​∑i=1N(f^​(𝐗i)−f∗​(𝐗i))2\left\|\hat{f}-f^{*}\right\|_{N}^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\hat{f}\left(\mathbf{X}_{i}\right)-f^{*}\left(\mathbf{X}_{i}\right)\right)^{2} (33)

The we can bound the L2​(PN)L^{2}\left(P_{N}\right)-norm between fτf_{\tau} (initialized with fPTf_{\text{PT}} ) and ftgtf_{\text{tgt}} as follows:

‖fτ−ftgt‖N2≤Bτ2+Vτ+Dτ2\left\|f_{\tau}-f_{\text{tgt}}\right\|_{N}^{2}\leq B_{\tau}^{2}+V_{\tau}+D_{\tau}^{2} (34)

where Bτ2B_{\tau}^{2} is the bias term, VτV_{\tau} is the variance term, and Dτ2D_{\tau}^{2} is the additional difference term. The key difference between the early stopping framework in Raskutti et al. [2014] and that in Sun and Raskutti [2025a] is that the latter accounts for modern non-linear models with evolving kernels during training, which introduce the extra error component Dτ2D_{\tau}^{2}.

According to Raskutti et al. [2014], for any iteration τ≤T^max\tau\leq\widehat{T}_{\max}, with certain probability, we can bound the sum of the bias and variance terms as

Bτ2+Vτ≤Cητ.B_{\tau}^{2}+V_{\tau}\leq\frac{C}{\eta_{\tau}}. (35)

Meanwhile, the difference term Dτ2D^{2}_{\tau} is non-decreasing in τ\tau. Suppose Dτ2D^{2}_{\tau} is upper bounded by a non-decreasing function g⁡(τ)g(\tau). Then the proposed optimal stopping time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} is defined as:

T^op:=argmin{τ≤T^max|Cητ+g(τ)}.\widehat{T}_{\text{op}}:=\arg\min\left\{\tau\leq\widehat{T}_{\max}\left\lvert\,\frac{C}{\eta_{\tau}}+g(\tau)\right.\right\}. (36)

For details of the proof of these intermediate results please refer to Sun and Raskutti [2025b] and Raskutti et al. [2014].

B.2 Network specification Details

For theoretical convenience, we set the embedding dimension for each layer dld^{l}, and the scaling factor dl,Gd^{l,G} to be the same as the network width nn. Same as Sun and Raskutti [2025a], we consider nn to be sufficiently large, so we can bound the error introduced by the evolving kernel during training, i.e. , the difference term Dτ2D^{2}_{\tau}. Note that we consider the number of heads dl,Hd^{l,H} to be finite, which is more realistic.

We use standard parameterization in the main paper and give theoretical results accordingly. But note that our results also hold for NTK parameterization, where we implicitly treat each weight Wi​j∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/n)W_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}/n\right), i.i.d., as W=σn​wW=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}w where only ww is trainable. For standard parameterization, we should normalize the NTK with the width or embedding dimension nn:

1n​⟨∇θf​(θ⁡(t),x),∇θf​(θ⁡(t),x′)⟩.\frac{1}{n}\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta(t),x\right),\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta(t),x^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle. (37)

And for the empirical kernel matrix KK, we denote 0<λmin:=λmin​(K)≤0<\lambda_{\min}:=\lambda_{\min}(K)\leq λmax:=λmax​(K)<∞\lambda_{\max}:=\lambda_{\max}(K)<\infty. And let ηcritical =2​(λmin+λmax)−1\eta_{\text{critical }}=2\left(\lambda_{\min}+\lambda_{\max}\right)^{-1}. Recall this empirical kernel matrix is defined on the target data 𝑿tgt\bm{X}^{\text{tgt}} and is the limit when the width and embedding dimension nn goes to ∞\infty:

limn→∞1n​⟨∇θf​(θ⁡(t),x),∇θf​(θ⁡(t),x′)⟩.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta(t),x\right),\nabla_{\theta}f\left(\theta(t),x^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle. (38)

We use standard parameterization in our proof, but note that the proof is almost the same for NTK parameterization with minor changes.

B.3 Extension to Transformer Decoder Based Network

B.3.1 Proof Overview

As discussed in the main paper, we consider two fine-tuning settings:

  1. 1.

    fFTf_{\text{FT}} and fPTf_{\text{PT}} share the same structure

  2. 2.

    An additional linear head can be appended to hidden layers of fPTf_{\text{PT}}

Consider setting 1 first, to extend results in Sun and Raskutti [2025b] for fully-connected networks, we need to prove two main conditions:

  1. i)

    The Jacobian is locally Lipschitz under random Gaussian initialization

  2. ii)

    The NTK at initialization, i.e., pretrained initialization in our setup, converges in probability to some analytic kernel Θ0\Theta_{0} as nn goes to ∞\infty.

Suppose we have already proven conditions i). Then we use the same proof strategy as in Sun and Raskutti [2025b], Sun and Raskutti [2025a] to derive the final mean prediction error convergence bound. The major steps of the proof strategy in Sun and Raskutti [2025b], Sun and Raskutti [2025a] is as follows:

  1. 1.

    With condition i) and the fact that the NTK of the network we consider converges in probability to some static kernel at random initialization as nn goes to ∞\infty [Yang, 2020b]22 2 Yang [2020b] states a general result for any network structure with random initialization., we can follow the same strategy of Theorem G.1 in Lee et al. [2019] to get the following results under random initialization:

    Theorem 3 (NTK convergence at random initialization).

    Under assumptions 4.1-4.7 in the main text, for γ>0\gamma>0 and η0<ηcritical \eta_{0}<\eta_{\text{critical }}, there exist R0>0,M∈ℕR_{0}>0,M\in\mathbb{N} and L>1L>1, such that for every m≥Mm\geq M, the following holds with probability at least (1−γ)\left(1-\gamma\right) starting from fPTf_{\text{PT}} or fPTkf^{k}_{\text{PT}} with an additional linear head added when applying gradient descent with learning rate ϵ=η0m\epsilon=\frac{\eta_{0}}{m} considering standard parameterization,

    {‖g⁡(θτ)‖2≤(1−η0​N1​λmin3)τ​R1∑j=1τ‖θj−θj−1‖2≤η0​K~​R1n​∑j=1τ(1−η0​N2​λmin3)j−1≤3​K~​R0N1​λmin​n−12\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\left\|g\left(\theta_{\tau}\right)\right\|_{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{\eta_{0}N_{1}\lambda_{\min}}{3}\right)^{\tau}R_{1}\\ \sum_{j=1}^{\tau}\left\|\theta_{j}-\theta_{j-1}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{\eta_{0}\tilde{K}R_{1}}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{\tau}\left(1-\frac{\eta_{0}N_{2}\lambda_{\min}}{3}\right)^{j-1}\leq\frac{3\tilde{K}R_{0}}{N_{1}\lambda_{\min}}n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\end{array}\right. (39)

    and

    supτ‖Krandom_init−Kτ‖F≤6​L3​R1N12​λmin​n−12\sup_{\tau}\left\|K_{\text{random\_init}}-K_{\tau}\right\|_{F}\leq\frac{6L^{3}R_{1}}{{N_{1}}^{2}\lambda_{\min}}n^{-\frac{1}{2}} (40)

    where K0K_{0} is the empirical kernel matrix induced by frandom_initf_{\text{random\_init}} and KτK_{\tau} is the one induced by fτf_{\tau} using pre-trained data 𝐗src\bm{X}^{\text{src}}.

    The second inequality in equation (39) shows that the parameter of fPTf_{\text{PT}} lies within O(n−1/2)O(n^{-1/2}) of some random initialization as illustrated in Figure 1. Note that the main difference between the above theorem and Theorem G.1 in Lee et al. [2019] is that our result applies to network architectures containing transformer blocks, whereas Theorem G.1 in Lee et al. [2019] is restricted to fully connected networks.

  2. 2.

    We use the fact that the parameters of fPTf_{\text{PT}} are within O(n−1/2)O(n^{-1/2}) of some random initialization, which is derived in previous step , along with the local Lipschitz property of the Jacobian under random normal initialization, to show that the Jacobian is also locally Lipschitz under pre-trained initialization. This reasoning is illustrated in Figure 1 and is essentially the same as the proof of Lemma 8 in Sun and Raskutti [2025b].

  3. 3.

    Because Krandom_initK_{\text{random\_init}} converges in probability to some static kernel [Yang, 2020b] and equation (40), condition ii) is satisfied. The key observation here is that for fine-tuning task we replace the data, but this is fine, as we assume both source dataset and target dataset are bounded, so even though the empirical NTK is evaluated on 𝑿src\bm{X}^{\text{src}}, the NTK convergence bound still holds for target dataset with some uniform constants changed. The detailed discussion regarding this can found in the proof of Theorem 3 in Sun and Raskutti [2025b]. Then we can use the same proof technique in the proof of Theorem 3 and 4 in Sun and Raskutti [2025b] to derive the NTK convergence under pretrained initialization (Theorem 5) and the network linearization (Lemma 6) in our setup.

  4. 4.

    The final step is to derive a bound on the mean prediction error under the optimal stopping time T^op\widehat{T}_{\text{op}} by following the same line of reasoning as in Theorem 2 and Corollary 2 of Sun and Raskutti [2025b]. The proof techniques developed in Sun and Raskutti [2025b] extend the methods of Raskutti et al. [2014] to enable a precise analysis of early stopping behavior in neural networks.

For setting 2, we need to we need to do a bit more work to handle the mix of random and non-random initialization, which is slightly different from the proof for setting 1. Additional proof details will be presented in later sections.

Remark B.1.

To apply the NTK results from [Yang, 2020b], we must first verify the following key assumption, which forms the theoretical foundation of those results:

Assumption B.1 (Simple GIA33 3 Gradient independence assumption: for any matrix WW, we assume W⊤W^{\top} used in backprop is independent from WW used in the forward pass. Check).

At initialization, the output layer of fPTf_{\text{PT}} is sampled independently and with zero mean from all other parameters and is not used anywhere else in the interior of the network.

Because our setting excludes architectures with shared weights (e.g., RNNs), the assumption holds automatically, allowing us to safely apply the results from Yang [2020b].

B.3.2 Local Lipschitzness for setting 1

We use θ\theta to denote the collections of all parameters for the network under consideration. And we use 𝒳\mathcal{X} to denote the training dataset, which may be a general dataset and is not restricted to the pre-trained source dataset. And for l≥1l\geq 1, let

δl​(θ,x):=∇fl​(θ,x)fL+1​(θ,x)∈ℝn\displaystyle\delta^{l}(\theta,x):=\nabla_{f^{l}(\theta,x)}f^{L+1}(\theta,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (41)
δl​(θ,𝒳):=∇fl​(θ,x)fL+1​(θ,𝒳)∈ℝ|𝒳|×(n×|𝒳|)\displaystyle\delta^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X}):=\nabla_{f^{l}(\theta,x)}f^{L+1}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}|\times(n\times|\mathcal{X}|)}

Recall that fl​(θ,x)f^{l}(\theta,x) is the pre-activation for layer ll.

The statement of the Lemma is as follows:

Lemma 2 (Standard parameterization).

There is a K~>0\tilde{K}>0 such that for every C>0C>0, with high probability over random initialization the following holds:

{1n​‖J⁡(θ)−J⁡(θ~)‖F≤H~​‖θ−θ~‖21n​‖J⁡(θ)‖F≤H,∀θ,θ~∈B(θ0,Cn−1/2)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|J(\theta)-J(\tilde{\theta})\|_{F}&\leq\tilde{H}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|J(\theta)\|_{F}&\leq H\end{array},\quad\forall\theta,\tilde{\theta}\in B\left(\theta_{0},Cn^{-1/2}\right)\right. (42)

where H~\tilde{H} means a quantity that is O⁡(logα⁡(n))O\left(\log^{\alpha}(n)\right).

Proof.

The core idea of proving this local lipschtiz is computing the gradient for each weight matrix and bound them directly. We adopt similar proof strategy as the proof of Lemma 1 in Lee et al. [2019].

We first consider adding only one attention layer without the residual connection (the ResNet structure). There are two main steps, the first is to bound the Jacobian of fully connected weights after introducing attention layer. The second is to bound to the Jacobian of attention weights themselves.

The proof of this Lemma relies on the below theorem to bound the operator norm of weight matrices:

Theorem 4 (Corollary 5.35 [Vershynin, 2010] ).

Let A=AN,nA=A_{N,n} be an N×nN\times n random matrix whose entries are independent standard normal random variables. Then for every t≥0t\geq 0, with probability at least 1−2exp(−t2/2)1-2\exp\left(-t^{2}/2\right) one has

N−n−t≤λmin​(A)≤λmax​(A)≤N+n+t.\sqrt{N}-\sqrt{n}-t\leq\lambda_{\min}(A)\leq\lambda_{\max}(A)\leq\sqrt{N}+\sqrt{n}+t. (43)

Let θ={Wl,bl,Wl,O,Wl,Q,Wl,K,Wl,V}\theta=\{W^{l},b^{l},W^{l,O},W^{l,Q},W^{l,K},W^{l,V}\} and θ~={W~l,b~l,W~l,O,W~l,Q,W~l,K,W~l,V}\tilde{\theta}=\{\tilde{W}_{l},\tilde{b}^{l},\tilde{W}^{l,O},\tilde{W}^{l,Q},\tilde{W}^{l,K},\tilde{W}^{l,V}\} be any two points in B⁡(θ0,C)B\left(\theta_{0},C\right). By the above theorem and the triangle inequality, we have w.h.p. over random initialization for the first layer weight matrices the operator norm ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}} is bounded by 3​σw​nn03\sigma_{w}\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n_{0}}}, for 2≤l≤L+12\leq l\leq L+1, ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}} is bounded by 3​σw3\sigma_{w}.

Fully connected weights.

To enable the same induction step for the fully connected layer weights, we first need to ensure that w.h.p. the following holds for the attention layer:

n−12​‖fl​(θ,𝒳)‖2,‖δl​(θ,𝒳)‖2≤K1n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left\|f^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\right\|_{2},\quad\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\right\|_{2}\leq K_{1} (44)
n−12​‖fl​(θ,𝒳)−fl​(θ~,𝒳)‖2≤K1​‖θ~−θ‖2n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left\|f^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})-f^{l}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right\|_{2}\leq K_{1}\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta\|_{2} (45)
‖δl​(θ,𝒳)−δl​(θ~,𝒳)‖2≤K~2​‖θ~−θ‖2\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})-\delta^{l}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right\|_{2}\leq\tilde{K}_{2}\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta\|_{2} (46)

where θ\theta and θ~\tilde{\theta} is any two points in B⁡(θ0,C)B\left(\theta_{0},C\right), K1K_{1} is some universal constants depend on |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| and LL, K~2\tilde{K}_{2} is some universal constant of order OPENO⁡(log⁡(nCLOSE))O(\sqrt{\log(n})). Note that in the following proofs, any constants related to |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| and LL are treated as 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1), we are only interested in and should be careful about the constants that grow w.r.t. nn.

We start by bounding ‖fl​(θ,x)‖2\left\|f^{l}(\theta,x)\right\|_{2}. Recall for each head, the output is calculated as

fl​h​(x)=ζ⁡(1dl,G​gl−1​(x)​Wl​h,Q​(gl−1​(x)​Wl​h,K)⊤)​gl−1​(x)​Wl​h,Vf^{lh}(x)=\zeta\left(\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}g^{l-1}(x)W^{lh,Q}\left(g^{l-1}(x)W^{lh,K}\right)^{\top}\right)g^{l-1}(x)W^{lh,V} (47)

We have known that

  • •

    the softmax matrix is of finite dimension and each entry is bounded

  • •

    by the induction step ‖gl−1​(x)‖2≤n1/2​K1\left\|g^{l-1}(x)\right\|_{2}\leq n^{1/2}K_{1}44 4 Assume all preceding layers are fully connected layer and use the same induction step as the (S85) in Lee et al. [2019].

  • •

    ‖Wl​h,V‖op≤3​σw\|W^{lh,V}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 3\sigma_{w} w.h.p.

then it is easy to see we can bound ‖fl​(θ,x)‖2\left\|f^{l}(\theta,x)\right\|_{2} as desired.

Next we bound δl​(θ,x)\delta^{l}(\theta,x). By back-prop recursion we know that

δl​(θ,x)=(δl+1​(θ,x)​Wl+1⊤)⊙ϕ′​(fl​(θ,x))\delta^{l}(\theta,x)=\left(\delta^{l+1}(\theta,x){W^{l+1}}^{\top}\right)\odot\phi^{\prime}\left(f^{l}(\theta,x)\right) (48)

again, use the induction step results in (S85) in Lee et al. [2019], it is not hard to bound δl​(θ,x)\delta^{l}(\theta,x).

We then proceed to show (45). By the definition of multi-head attention, we have

‖fl​(θ,𝒳)−fl​(θ~,𝒳)‖2\displaystyle\|f^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})-f^{l}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\|_{2} =∥∑hfl​h((θ,x)Wl​h,O−∑hfl​h(θ~,𝒳)W~l​h,O∥2\displaystyle=\|\sum_{h}f^{lh}((\theta,x)W^{lh,O}-\sum_{h}f^{lh}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\tilde{W}^{lh,O}\|_{2} (49)
≤∑h∥fl​h((θ,𝒳)Wl​h,O−fl​h(θ~,𝒳)W~l​h,O∥2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{h}\|f^{lh}((\theta,\mathcal{X})W^{lh,O}-f^{lh}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\tilde{W}^{lh,O}\|_{2}

Since we consider the number of head to be finite, it suffices to prove the lipschtzness for one single head. After using the add and subtract tricks and all the proved bounds, the major thing left to prove is the lipschtzness of the pre-softmax quantity of the attention layer. Denote A=1dl,G​Q​KTA=\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}QK^{T}, where Q=gl−1​(x)​Wl​h,Q,K=gl−1​(x)​Wl​h,KQ=g^{l-1}(x)W^{lh,Q},K=g^{l-1}(x)W^{lh,K}. Let Δ​Q:=gl−1​Wl​h,Q−g~l−1​W~l​h,Q\Delta Q:=g^{l-1}W^{lh,Q}-\tilde{g}^{l-1}\tilde{W}^{lh,Q}, we have

‖Δ​Q‖2\displaystyle\|\Delta Q\|_{2} ≤‖gl−1‖2​‖Wl​h,Q−W~l​h,Q‖F+‖Wl​h,Q‖o​p​‖gl−1−g~l−1‖2\displaystyle\leq\|g^{l-1}\|_{2}\|W^{lh,Q}-\tilde{W}^{lh,Q}\|_{F}+\|W^{lh,Q}\|_{op}\|g^{l-1}-\tilde{g}^{l-1}\|_{2} (50)
≤O⁡(n1/2)​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\leq O(n^{1/2})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}

where we use the induction result on ‖gl−1−g~l−1‖\|g^{l-1}-\tilde{g}^{l-1}\|, which is simply the (S85) in Lee et al. [2019]. Similarly, for Δ​K\Delta K, we have the same bound. Combine, we have

‖Δ​A‖2\displaystyle\|\Delta A\|_{2} ≤1dl,G​‖Δ​Q‖2⋅O⁡(n1/2)⋅‖Wl​h,K‖o​p+1dl,G​‖Δ​K‖2⋅O⁡(n1/2)⋅‖Wl​h,Q‖o​p\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\|\Delta Q\|_{2}\cdot O(n^{1/2})\cdot\|W^{lh,K}\|_{op}+\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\|\Delta K\|_{2}\cdot O(n^{1/2})\cdot\|W^{lh,Q}\|_{op} (51)
≤O⁡(n)dl,G​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\leq\frac{O(n)}{d^{l,G}}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}
=O⁡(1)​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle=O(1)\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}

where we use the fact that ∥gl−1∥2∥\|g^{l-1}\|_{2}\| is O⁡(n1/2)O(n^{1/2}) and dl,G=nd^{l,G}=n.

Finally, we prove (46). The proof is the similar to the proof of (S86) in Lee et al. [2019]. The only difference is that during the induction step and while bounding this term, we will encounter a term as below

δl+1​(θ~)​Wl+1⊤⊙(ϕ′​(fl​(θ,𝒳))−ϕ′​(fl​(θ~,𝒳)))(A)\delta^{l+1}(\tilde{\theta}){W^{l+1}}^{\top}\odot\left(\phi^{\prime}\left(f^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\right)-\phi^{\prime}\left(f^{l}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right)\right)\quad({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}A}) (52)

We bound it as follows

‖(A)‖2\displaystyle\|({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}A})\|_{2} ≤‖δl+1​(θ~)​Wl+1⊤‖∞​‖ϕ′​(fl​(θ,𝒳))−ϕ′​(fl​(θ~,𝒳))‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\delta^{l+1}(\tilde{\theta}){W^{l+1}}^{\top}\|_{\infty}\|\phi^{\prime}\left(f^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\right)-\phi^{\prime}\left(f^{l}(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right)\|_{2} (53)
≤O⁡(‖δl+1‖2​log⁡(n)n1/2)​O​(n1/2)​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\leq O\left(\|\delta^{l+1}\|_{2}\frac{\sqrt{\log(n)}}{n^{1/2}}\right)O(n^{1/2})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}
=O~​(1)​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle=\tilde{O}(1)\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}

where we use induction results regarding δl\delta^{l} and flf^{l} and assumption about the activation function. For ‖δl+1​Wl+1⊤‖∞\|\delta^{l+1}{W^{l+1}}^{\top}\|_{\infty}, observe that condition on δl+1\delta^{l+1}, each entry is a Gaussian random variable 𝒩⁡(0,‖δl+1‖22n)\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{\|\delta^{l+1}\|_{2}^{2}}{n}), so we can bound it using the tail probability of Gaussian variable to get the O⁡(‖δl+1‖2​log⁡(n)n1/2)O\left(\|\delta^{l+1}\|_{2}\frac{\sqrt{\log(n)}}{n^{1/2}}\right) bound. Note that here we need to make use of the GIA assumption mentioned in Remark B.1.

Besides these, we need to bound ∂fl∂gl−1\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}} and prove its lipstchzness to enable the same induction proof on fully connected layer weights. This is crucial because for the layer before the attention layer

δl−1​(θ)=δl​(θ)​∂fl∂gl−1.\delta^{l-1}(\theta)=\delta^{l}(\theta)\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}}. (54)

We define the intermediate quantities to facilitate the calculation of this gradient:

Qh=gl−1Wl​h,Q,Kh=gl−1Wl​h,K,V=XWl​h,V,\displaystyle Q_{h}=g^{l-1}W^{lh,Q},\quad K_{h}=g^{l-1}W^{lh,K},\quad V=XW^{lh,V}, (55)
Sh=1dl,GQhKh⊤,Ph=softmaxrows(Sh),Ah=PhVh,\displaystyle S_{h}=\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}Q_{h}K_{h}^{\top},\quad P_{h}=\operatorname{softmax}_{\mathrm{rows}}(S_{h}),\quad A_{h}=P_{h}V_{h},
Λh=block​_​diag(Λh,0,…,Λh,T−1)∈ℝT2×T2,Λh,i=diag(Ph,i:)−Ph,i:Ph,i:⊤.\displaystyle\Lambda_{h}=\operatorname{block\_diag}\left(\Lambda_{h,0},\ldots,\Lambda_{h,T-1}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{2}\times T^{2}},\quad\Lambda_{h,i}=\operatorname{diag}\left(P_{h,i:}\right)-P_{h,i:}P_{h,i:}^{\top}.

Then we have for each head, we denote ∂fl​h∂gl−1∈ℝ(T​n)×(T​n)\frac{\partial f^{lh}}{\partial g^{l-1}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\left(Tn\right)\times\left(Tn\right)} as JhJ^{h}

Jh=WhV⊤⊗Ph+1dl,G​(In⊗Vh⊤)​Λh​[(Kh⊗IT)​(Wl​h,Q​T⊗IT)+(IT⊗Qh)​(Wl​h,K⊤⊗IT)].J^{h}=W_{h}^{V\top}\otimes P_{h}+\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\left(I_{n}\otimes V_{h}^{\top}\right)\Lambda_{h}\left[\left(K_{h}\otimes I_{T}\right)\left(W^{lh,QT}\otimes I_{T}\right)+\left(I_{T}\otimes Q_{h}\right)\left(W^{lh,K\top}\otimes I_{T}\right)\right]. (56)

Then the final gradient is

∂fl∂gl−1=(Wl,O⊤⊗IT)​(⨁h=1HJh)∈ℝ(T​n)×(T​n)\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}}=\left(W^{l,O\top}\otimes I_{T}\right)\left(\bigoplus_{h=1}^{H}J^{h}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{\left(Tn\right)\times\left(Tn\right)} (57)

Use same argument as above, it is not hard to show that

‖∂fl∂gl−1‖F≤O(1),‖∂fl∂gl−1(θ,x)−∂fl∂gl−1(θ~,x)‖F≤O(1)∥θ−θ~∥2.\displaystyle\left\|\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}}\right\|_{F}\leq O(1),\left\|\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}}(\theta,x)-\frac{\partial f^{l}}{\partial g^{l-1}}(\tilde{\theta},x)\right\|_{F}\leq O(1)\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}. (58)

Note that we use pooling operation after the attention layer, since we assume they are simple deterministic reduction operation, and we only operate on finite dimension, this would not affect the above proved results.

Attention weights.

For each attention weights, the goal is to bound the Jacobian of itself and also prove the lipstchzness.

We start with Wl,OW^{l,O}. Note that

J⁡(Wl,O)=[fl​1​(x),…,fl​dl,H​(x)]T​δl​(θ,x)J(W^{l,O})=\left[f^{l1}(x),\ldots,f^{ld^{l,H}}(x)\right]^{T}\delta^{l}(\theta,x) (59)

Then it is not hard to prove that

‖[fl​1​(𝒳),…,fl​dl,H​(𝒳)]T​δl​(θ,𝒳)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2)\displaystyle\left\|\left[f^{l1}(\mathcal{X}),\ldots,f^{ld^{l,H}}(\mathcal{X})\right]^{T}\delta^{l}(\theta,\mathcal{X})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}) (60)
‖J⁡(Wl,O)​(θ,𝒳)−J⁡(Wl,O)​(θ~,𝒳)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2​log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2.\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{l,O})(\theta,\mathcal{X})-J(W^{l,O})(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}\sqrt{\log(n)})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}.

Next for Wl​h,VW^{lh,V}, we have

J⁡(Wl​h,V)=gl−1⊤​PhT​∂fL+1∂fl​h​Wl​h,O​TJ(W^{lh,V})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}P_{h}^{T}\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial f^{lh}}W^{lh,OT} (61)

where ∂fL+1∂fl​h=δl​(θ,x)​Wl​h,O⊤\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial f^{lh}}=\delta^{l}(\theta,x){W^{lh,O}}^{\top}.

Similarly, we can show that

‖J⁡(Wl​h,V)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2)\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,V})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}) (62)
‖J⁡(Wl​h,V)​(θ,x)−J⁡(Wl​h,V)​(θ~,x)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2​log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2.\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,V})(\theta,x)-J(W^{lh,V})(\tilde{\theta},x)\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}\sqrt{\log(n)})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}.

Finally, for query and key matrices, we have

J⁡(Wl​h,Q)=gl−1⊤⋅(1dl,G⋅∂Ph∂Sh⊤⋅∂fL+1∂Ph⋅Kh)\displaystyle J(W^{lh,Q})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\cdot{\frac{\partial P_{h}}{\partial S_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial P_{h}}\cdot K^{h}\right) (63)
J⁡(Wl​h,K)=gl−1⊤⋅(1dl,G⋅∂fL+1∂Ph⊤⋅∂Ph∂Sh⊤⋅Qh)\displaystyle J(W^{lh,K})={g^{l-1}}^{\top}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{d^{l,G}}\cdot{\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial P_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot{\frac{\partial P_{h}}{\partial S_{h}}}^{\top}\cdot Q^{h}\right)

where ∂fL+1∂Ph=∂fL+1∂fl​h​Vh⊤\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial P_{h}}=\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial f^{lh}}{V^{h}}^{\top} and ∂Ph∂Sh⊤{\frac{\partial P_{h}}{\partial S_{h}}}^{\top} is simply Λh\Lambda_{h} defined in (55).

We can show that the following holds for these two types of weights by similar reasoning as above:

‖J⁡(Wl​h,Q)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2)\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,Q})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}) (64)
‖J⁡(Wl​h,Q)​(θ,𝒳)−J⁡(Wl​h,Q)​(θ~,𝒳)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2​log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,Q})(\theta,\mathcal{X})-J(W^{lh,Q})(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}\sqrt{\log(n)})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}
‖J⁡(Wl​h,K)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2)\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,K})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2})
‖J⁡(Wl​h,K)​(θ,𝒳)−J⁡(Wl​h,K)​(θ~,𝒳)‖F≤O⁡(n1/2​log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2.\displaystyle\left\|J(W^{lh,K})(\theta,\mathcal{X})-J(W^{lh,K})(\tilde{\theta},\mathcal{X})\right\|_{F}\leq O(n^{1/2}\sqrt{\log(n)})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}.

The results of Lemma 89 follows from the above estimates, we just sum all together to get the desired bound

1n​‖J⁡(θ)‖F2\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|J(\theta)\|_{F}^{2} =∑l‖1n​J​(Wl)‖F2+‖J⁡(bl)‖F2⏟fully connected layers+∑l‖1n​J​(Wl,O)‖F2+∑l,h,∙={K,Q,V}‖1n​J​(Wl​h,∙)‖F2⏟attention layer weights\displaystyle=\underbrace{\sum_{l}\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}J\left(W^{l}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|J\left(b^{l}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{fully connected layers}}+\underbrace{\sum_{l}\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}J\left(W^{l,O}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,h,\bullet=\{K,Q,V\}\end{subarray}}\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}J\left(W^{lh,\bullet}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{attention layer weights}} (65)
=1n​∑l∑x∈𝒳‖gl−1​(θ,x)​δl​(θ,x)T‖F2+‖δl​(θ,x)T‖F2+O⁡(1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{l}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left\|g^{l-1}(\theta,x)\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}+O(1)
≤1n​∑l∑x∈𝒳(1+‖gl−1​(θ,x)‖F2)​‖δl​(θ,x)T‖F2+O⁡(1)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{l}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left(1+\left\|g^{l-1}(\theta,x)\right\|_{F}^{2}\right)\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}+O(1)
≤∑l1n​(1+K12​n)​∑x‖δl​(θ,x)T‖F2+O⁡(1)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{l}\frac{1}{n}\left(1+K_{1}^{2}n\right)\sum_{x}\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}+O(1)
≤∑l1n​K12​(1+K12​n)+O⁡(1)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{l}\frac{1}{n}K_{1}^{2}\left(1+K_{1}^{2}n\right)+O(1)
≤2​(L+1)​K14+O⁡(1)\displaystyle\leq 2(L+1)K_{1}^{4}+O(1)
=O⁡(1)\displaystyle=O(1)

Similarly, for the lipschitzness

‖J⁡(θ)−J⁡(θ~)‖F2\displaystyle\|J(\theta)-J(\tilde{\theta})\|_{F}^{2} =∑l∑x∈𝒳‖1n​gl−1​(θ,x)​δl​(θ,x)T−1n​gl−1​(θ~,x)​δl​(θ~,x)T‖F2+‖δl​(θ,x)T−δl​(θ~,x)T‖F2⏟fully connected layers\displaystyle=\underbrace{\sum_{l}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}g^{l-1}(\theta,x)\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}g^{l-1}(\tilde{\theta},x)\delta^{l}(\tilde{\theta},x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|\delta^{l}(\theta,x)^{T}-\delta^{l}(\tilde{\theta},x)^{T}\right\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{fully connected layers}} (66)
+∑l1n​‖J⁡(Wl,O,θ)−J⁡(Wl,O,θ~)‖F2+∑l,h,∙={K,Q,V}1n​‖J⁡(Wl​h,∙,θ)−J⁡(Wl​h,∙,θ~)‖F2⏟attention layer weights\displaystyle+\underbrace{\sum_{l}\frac{1}{n}\left\|J\left(W^{l,O},\theta\right)-J\left(W^{l,O},\tilde{\theta}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,h,\bullet=\{K,Q,V\}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}\left\|J\left(W^{lh,\bullet},\theta\right)-J\left(W^{lh,\bullet},\tilde{\theta}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{attention layer weights}}
≤(∑l4​K12​K~12+K~12)​‖θ−θ~‖2+O⁡(log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{l}4K_{1}^{2}\tilde{K}_{1}^{2}+\tilde{K}_{1}^{2}\right)\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}+O(\log(n))\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}
≤3​(L+1)​K12​K~12​‖θ−θ~‖2+O⁡(log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2\displaystyle\leq 3(L+1)K_{1}^{2}\tilde{K}_{1}^{2}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}+O(\log(n))\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}
=O⁡(log⁡(n))​‖θ−θ~‖2.\displaystyle=O(\log(n))\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}.

We then extend the results to transformer block. By definition, the transformer output is

zl\displaystyle z^{l} =gl−1+multi-head attention layer​(gl−1)\displaystyle=g^{l-1}+\text{multi-head attention layer}(g^{l-1}) (67)
fl​(x)\displaystyle f^{l}(x) =zl+fully connected layer​(zl).\displaystyle=z^{l}+\text{fully connected layer}(z^{l}).

Since we already prove the results for multi-head attention layer, by the above formula, it is trivial to extend all these results to transformer block using the same proof strategy.

Also, we can easily extend the above results to network with multiple transformer blocks by induction. The only left component in the transformer decoder is the LayerNorm. We consider the specific steps to deal with is as below.

LayerNorm.

For theoretical convenience, we give the proof for the case where the sequence length is 1, since TT is finite, the result can be easily extended to standard situation. Given an LayerNorm input vector x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (for one token), LayerNorm first computes mean and variance as follows:

μ=1n​∑i=1nxi,σ2=1n​∑i=1n(xi−μ)2\mu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i},\ \ \sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}-\mu)^{2} (68)

and then normalize and add learnable parameters:

x^i=xi−μσ2+ϵ,yi=γi​x^i+βi.\hat{x}_{i}=\frac{x_{i}-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}},\ \ y_{i}=\gamma_{i}\hat{x}_{i}+\beta_{i}. (69)

The final output is given by

y=γ⊙x−μσ2+ϵ+βy=\gamma\odot\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}}+\beta (70)

where γ,β∈ℝn\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{n} are learnable parameters, and ϵ\epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. Note xx is the output of some preceding layers. After introducing LayerNorm to the network, the Jacobian of some of the weights will be affected, so in order to maintain the same Lipschitz norm, we need to prove the following two main conditions hold w.h.p.:

  1. 1.
    ‖∂fL+1∂x‖2≤𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\left\|\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial x}\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n}) (71)
  2. 2.
    ‖∂fL+1∂x​(θ)−∂fL+1∂x​(θ~)‖2≤𝒪⁡(log⁡n)​‖θ−θ~‖2\left\|\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial x}(\theta)-\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial x}(\tilde{\theta})\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n})\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2} (72)

We start by proving equation (71). Let δi\delta_{i} denote upstream gradient ∂fL+1∂yi\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial y_{i}}, and u~i\tilde{u}_{i} denote ui​γiu_{i}\gamma_{i}, then we can write:

∂fL+1∂x=1σ2+ϵ​[δ~−mean​(δ~)⋅𝟏−mean​(δ~⊙x~)⋅x~]\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}}\left[\tilde{\delta}-\text{mean}(\tilde{\delta})\cdot\mathbf{1}-\text{mean}(\tilde{\delta}\odot\tilde{x})\cdot\tilde{x}\right] (73)

where x~,δ,δ~∈ℝn\tilde{x},\delta,\tilde{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} ,𝟏\mathbf{1} is an all-one vector of length nn, and mean​(v)=1n​∑jvj\text{mean}(v)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}v_{j}. Observe that

1σ2+ϵ≤1ϵ\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon}} (74)

and

≤‖δ~‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\tilde{\delta}\|_{2}
≤‖γ‖∞​‖δ‖2≤𝒪⁡(log⁡n)​𝒪​(1).\displaystyle\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}\|\delta\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n})\mathcal{O}(1).

Combine results (74) (75) (77) (80), we can get (71).

Now we turn to prove (72). We use the same add and subtract trick which is commonly used in this proof. And there is a term related to σ\sigma, and we need to show that

Next we write σ\sigma with projection matrix P:=𝟏−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤P:=\mathbf{1}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}, then we have

σ2​(x)=1n​∑j(xj−μ⁡(x))2=1n​‖P​x‖22.\sigma^{2}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}(x_{j}-\mu(x))^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\|Px\|_{2}^{2}. (83)

Then we have

|σ2−σ~2|\displaystyle|\sigma^{2}-\tilde{\sigma}^{2}| =1n​|‖P​x‖22−‖P​x~‖22|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\left|\|Px\|_{2}^{2}-\|P\tilde{x}\|_{2}^{2}\right| (84)
=1n​|(P​x+P​x~)⊤​(P​x−P​x~)|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\left|{(Px+P\tilde{x})}^{\top}(Px-P\tilde{x})\right|
≤1n​‖P⁡(x−x~)‖2​(‖P​x‖2+‖P​x~‖2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\|P(x-\tilde{x})\|_{2}(\|Px\|_{2}+\|P\tilde{x}\|_{2})
≤1n​‖x−x~‖2​(‖P​x‖2+‖P​x~‖2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}(\|Px\|_{2}+\|P\tilde{x}\|_{2})

where we use the fact that PP is orthogonal projection and ‖P​z‖2≤‖z‖2\|Pz\|_{2}\leq\|z\|_{2}. Next since ‖P​x‖2=n​σ2​(x)\|Px\|_{2}=\sqrt{n\sigma^{2}(x)}, we can write

|σ2−σ~2|≤1n​‖x−x~‖2​(σ2​(x)+σ2​(x~)).|\sigma^{2}-\tilde{\sigma}^{2}|\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}\left(\sqrt{\sigma^{2}(x)}+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}(\tilde{x})}\right). (85)

Use the fact that σ2​(x)≤1n​‖x‖22\sigma^{2}(x)\leq\frac{1}{n}\|x\|_{2}^{2} and ‖x‖2≤O⁡(n)\|x\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{n}), we have

σ2​(x)+σ2​(x~)≤2​O​(n)n=O⁡(1)\sqrt{\sigma^{2}(x)}+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}(\tilde{x})}\leq\frac{2O(\sqrt{n})}{\sqrt{n}}=O(1) (86)

finally, we get

|σ2−σ~2|≤O⁡(n)n​‖θ−θ~‖2=O⁡(1)​‖θ−θ~‖2.|\sigma^{2}-\tilde{\sigma}^{2}|\leq\frac{O(\sqrt{n})}{\sqrt{n}}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}=O(1)\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}. (87)

where we use the induction result w.r.t. xx.

The gradient w.r.t. γ\gamma and β\beta is given by

∂fL+1∂γ\displaystyle\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial\gamma} =∂fL+1∂y⊙x~\displaystyle=\frac{\partial f^{L+1}}{\partial y}\odot\tilde{x} (88)

we can prove the desired bound for these gradients and their Lipschitzness with similar reasoning steps as above.

Note that here we consider full batch gradient descent, and we do not write out the summation over training samples 𝒳\mathcal{X} explicitly as this will only add a constant related to |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| in the final bound, wich we simply view them as O⁡(1)O(1). And this concludes our proof.

The local Lipschitzness for the NTK parameterization is as follows:

Lemma 3 (NTK parameterization).

There is a L~>0\tilde{L}>0 such that for every C>0C>0, with high probability over random initialization θ0\theta_{0} the following holds:

{‖J⁡(θ)−J⁡(θ~)‖F≤H~​‖θ−θ~‖2‖J⁡(θ)‖F≤H,∀θ,θ~∈B⁡(θ0,C)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\|J(\theta)-J(\tilde{\theta})\|_{F}&\leq\tilde{H}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}\\ \|J(\theta)\|_{F}&\leq H\end{array},\quad\forall\theta,\tilde{\theta}\in B\left(\theta_{0},C\right)\right. (89)

B.4 Proof for Setting 2

We formally state the fine-tuning setting 2 as follows: take the kk-th hidden layer of the pretrained network fPTf_{\text{PT}} as backbone denoted by fPTkf_{\text{PT}}^{k}, we append a linear head after it. We denote the parameter of this linear head as {W,b}\{W,b\}, with Wi​j∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/n),b∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)W_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}/n\right),\ b\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}\right).

Lemma 4.

There is a L>0L>0 such that for every C>0C>0, with high probability the following holds over the special mixed initialization described above :

{1n​‖J⁡(θ)−J⁡(θ~)‖F≤L~​‖θ−θ~‖21n​‖J⁡(θ)‖F≤L,∀θ,θ~∈B(θ0,Cn−1/2)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|J(\theta)-J(\tilde{\theta})\|_{F}&\leq\tilde{L}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|J(\theta)\|_{F}&\leq L\end{array},\quad\forall\theta,\tilde{\theta}\in B\left(\theta_{0},Cn^{-1/2}\right)\right. (90)

where θ0\theta_{0} denote the initial parameter values of linear head, which is sampled from random Gaussian, and the backbone, which inherit the pretrained parameters.

Denote the parameter of the initial backbone part as θBackBone0\theta^{0}_{\text{BackBone}} and the initial parameter of linear head as {Wr.i.,br.i.}\{W^{r.i.},b^{r.i.}\}. Then for any θ∈B(θ0,Cn−1/2)\theta\in B\left(\theta_{0},Cn^{-1/2}\right), we have w.h.p.

+‖θBackBone−θBackBone0‖+‖θBackBoner.i.−θBackBone0‖\displaystyle+\|\theta_{\text{BackBone}}-\theta^{0}_{\text{BackBone}}\|+\|\theta^{r.i.}_{\text{BackBone}}-\theta^{0}_{\text{BackBone}}\|
≤(C1+C)n−1/2\displaystyle\leq(C_{1}+C)n^{-1/2}

Therefore we have shown that both θ~,θ∈B(θ0r.i.,Cn−1/2)\tilde{\theta},\theta\in B\left(\theta^{r.i.}_{0},Cn^{-1/2}\right), where θ0r.i.\theta^{r.i.}_{0} is the random initialization of this network we have considered in this paper. So make use of Lemma 89 again, we concludes our proof.

Lemma 5.

For this particular setting described above, the NTK converges to some analytical kernel as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

Denote the backbone part as fBackBonef_{\text{BackBone}}, then the NTK w.r.t the linear head WW is
